keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 907 alone (Cliopatria starts Qi in 911). Cliopatria's shape (Pingliang, southern Ningxia, eastern Gansu) leaves out the capital Fengxiang: Baoji falls wholly inside its Former Shu shape. Added from the Li Maozhen page: Baoda (保大) and Baosai (保塞), 'headquartered in modern Yan'an', held by Qi until 'both surrendered to Later Liang' in late 908; Jingnan (靜難, 'headquartered in modern Xianyang'), whose Li Jihui 'resubmitted to Li Maozhen' in 904 and stayed Qi's until Li Baoheng 'surrendered Jingnan Circuit to Later Liang' in 915. The Yan'an and Jingnan discs (80 and 40 km) are readings of 'the circuit'; the page gives no boundary. The Pingliang-Ningxia part is unverified (the Li Maozhen page is silent on it beyond Zhangyi, 'headquartered in modern Pingliang', whose governor Liu Zhijun Qi appointed in winter 908).

Cliopatria's 94,436 km2 contains no Fengxiang, and 13 of the 55 cells of the three Jingnan discs (Qing and part of Ning); the rest of Jingnan lies in its Later Liang shape. The Qi page gives no area and only says that at its prime the state 'covered parts of modern-day Gansu, Shaanxi, and Sichuan provinces'.

Fengxiang itself fell only to siege in 916 and was relieved. The Tianshui disc is taken out explicitly because 4,805 km2 of it lies inside Cliopatria's Qi shape.

Cliopatria's northern part (Pingliang, Guyuan, southern Ningxia) is dropped; the Li Maozhen and Zhu Wen pages are silent on who held it after 915.

ledger.note: 907: Li Maozhen's Qi is established at Fengxiang. Infobox 'Established: 907'; he had been created Prince of Qi in 901 and kept the Tang era name. The page names the capital, not a boundary.

region.text: the Baoda (保大) and Baosai (保塞) circuits, both headquartered in modern Yan'an

ledger.note: Late 908: Baoda and Baosai surrender to Later Liang. 'The Baosai officer Gao Wanxing (高萬興) ... and the Qi military governor of Baoda, Li Yanbo (李彥博), both surrendered to Later Liang'; Baoda is '保大, headquartered in modern Yan'an' and Baosai '保塞, headquartered in modern Yan'an'. The page gives no month for the surrender; the Yan'an disc is a reading of the two circuits.

region.text: Qin Prefecture, the Tianxiong circuit's seat

ledger.note: 915: Qin and Feng prefectures fall to Shu. 'In fall 915, Wang Jian launched a major attack against Qi. Feng Prefecture fell, and Li Jichong surrendered Qin.' The page does not locate the prefectures; Qin is read as the Tianshui country.

region.text: the Jingnan Circuit (靜難), the Bin, Ning and Qing prefectures

ledger.note: 915: the Jingnan Circuit goes to Later Liang. 'In 915, Li Jihui's adoptive son Li Baoheng (李保衡) killed Li Yanlu and surrendered Jingnan Circuit to Later Liang' (Jingnan '靜難, headquartered in modern Xianyang'); Zhu Zhen gave it to his general Huo Yanwei, and 'Qi was unable to regain Jingnan thereafter'. The page does not name the prefectures: Bin, Ning and Qing are the Jingnan circuit's three prefectures, drawn as three 40 km discs.
916: Shu storms Baoji and besieges Fengxiang. 'In fall 916, Wang Jian prepared another major attack against Qi'; Baoji was captured and Fengxiang besieged.

region.text: the Baoji country outside the Fengxiang core

ledger.note: 916: Baoji is lost to Shu. The page says Baoji was captured and does not say it was returned, so it stays with Shu (a reading); the Li Maozhen page says Qi's territory was now limited to Fengxiang and its immediate surroundings.

region.text: the Pingliang-Guyuan-Ningxia part of Cliopatria's Qi shape, which no opened page ties to Qi after 915

ledger.note: 916: the rest of Cliopatria's Qi shape is dropped. 'Qi's territory was limited to Fengxiang Municipality and its immediate surroundings' (fall 916). Whom the Pingliang-Guyuan-Ningxia country belonged to afterwards is on no opened page: the Li Maozhen page gives only Zhangyi ('headquartered in modern Pingliang'), whose governor Liu Zhijun Qi appointed in winter 908 and who 'fled to Former Shu' after the Qin surrender, and the Zhu Wen page is silent on Pingliang, Zhangyi, Guyuan and Jingyuan. The Jingnan part went to Later Liang in 915 (the event above), the Baoda and Baosai part in 908. The remainder is recorded as stateless (a bridging judgment).

region.text: Fengxiang, where the siege was lifted

ledger.note: 916: Shu lifts the siege of Fengxiang. 'The siege, however, was hampered by snowstorms, and Wang Jian decided to lift the siege.'

924: Qi submits to the Later Tang. 'In spring 924, Li Maozhen sent his son Li Jiyan' to submit tribute and a petition calling himself a Later Tang subject; Li Jiyan was confirmed as military governor of Fengxiang by Emperor Zhuangzong. No battle.

region.text: Fengxiang, submitted to the Later Tang

ledger.note: 924: the Qi principality ends. Infobox 'Disestablished: 924'; Li Maozhen died 17 May 924 (Li Maozhen page); the Five Dynasties page: 'In 924, Li Cunxu received the submission of Shaanxi's Qi kingdom'. The land passes to the Later Tang.

wars.name: Shu-Qi war
wars.outcome: Shu victory: Qin and Feng prefectures in autumn 915, Baoji in autumn 916; the siege of Fengxiang was lifted, leaving Qi only the country round its capital.
wars.note: 'In 911, though, the Shu-Qi alliance would break up over marital relations'; Li Maozhen's 910 request for Ba and Jian prefectures was refused. Late 911: 'Shu forces were able to decisively defeat Qi forces, forcing them to withdraw'.

wars.name: Joint Qi-Shu attack on Chang'an
wars.outcome: Failed: 'Qi forces were defeated by Liu Zhijun at Mu Valley'; Jin's relief of Zhaoyi went ahead without Qi aid. No border moved.

wars.name: Qi-Jin attack on Dingnan Circuit
wars.outcome: Failed: Qi allied with Jin against Later Liang's Dingnan Circuit, but 'Later Liang's relief forces made them withdraw'.

wars.name: Qi-Later Liang border war

wars.outcome: Later Liang gains: Baoda and Baosai (Yan'an) surrender in late 908 and the Jingnan Circuit in 915. Qi's counter-moves failed: Liu Zhijun's 909 raid on Chang'an was undone, the 910 attack on Dingnan with Jin was driven off, and an attempt to retake Jingnan 'initially resulted in a stalemate'.
wars.note: Zhu Wen page (second page, 909 sentence only): Liu Zhijun 'surrendering not only his own Zhongwu Circuit to Qi but also capturing Chang'an'; the page is silent on Pingliang, Zhangyi, Bin, Ning, Qing and Yan'an.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line is on any page. The Fengxiang core is a named city; the northern and western edges Cliopatria draws are unverified, and the frontiers moved in 908 (Later Liang, Yan'an), 915 (Shu, Later Liang) and 916 (Shu).

notes: The brief and the earlier Cliopatria discussions name the son Li Jiqian; every opened page says Li Jiyan, renamed Li Congyan in 926 (the Qi page infobox even mixes the two). The identity's successor note therefore says 'Li Jiyan (later Li Congyan)'. Cliopatria's Qi shape (94,436 km2: Pingliang, southern Ningxia, eastern Gansu; 62 percent of Ningxia, 12 percent of Gansu, 4 percent of Shaanxi) does not contain Fengxiang (Baoji): the same cells belong to Cliopatria's Former Shu shape from 911, and the Later Jin 936 and Later Tang 926 shapes absorb the Qi shape with no gap. The pages do not mention Pingliang or Jingyuan at all; this dossier keeps the Cliopatria part until 915 (unverified) and removes it in 916, when the Li Maozhen page says Qi was 'limited to Fengxiang Municipality and its immediate surroundings', recording the land as stateless (confidence 1). If a gap-filler finds who held Pingliang and southern Ningxia in 916-925 (Later Liang's Jingyuan, the Tibetans or the Dangxiang), the ledger event at index 4 should name them. Zhu Quanzhong's 902-903 siege of Fengxiang and the 901-902 losses of Jingnan (Binzhou), Wuding/Shannan West and Baoda predate the state and are not in the ledger. The Qi page gives no area; with the correction the state is about 2,800 km2 from 916 (a 30 km disc). Gazetteer names wanted: place Fengxiang (Baoji, Shaanxi), used as a coordinate disc. FIX ROUND (2026-10-19): the reviewer found two Later Liang gains from Qi that this dossier lacked, both on the Li Maozhen page: Baoda and Baosai (Yan'an) in late 908 and the Jingnan Circuit (Bin, Ning, Qing; 'headquartered in modern Xianyang') in 915. Both are now loss events (counterpart later-liang-dynasty) and the keyframes are 907 (with Yan'an), 908-910, 911-914, 915 (without Qin and Jingnan), 916-921, 922-924. Cliopatria's Qi shape contains no Bin or Ning cell and only 13 of the 55 cells of the three Jingnan discs (Qing); its Later Liang shape contains all of Yan'an and the rest of Jingnan. The 915 keyframe now also removes the Tianshui disc (Qin Prefecture, 4,805 km2 of Cliopatria's Qi shape) as the reviewer asked. The 916 stateless remainder (Pingliang, Guyuan, Ningxia) is still on no page: the Zhu Wen page is silent on Pingliang, Zhangyi and Guyuan, and the Li Maozhen page only has Liu Zhijun made governor of Zhangyi in winter 908 and fleeing to Shu after 915; the event stays at confidence 1. Radii (40 km for each Jingnan prefecture, 80 km for Yan'an) are the author's readings; the gazetteer lacks the places Bin, Ning, Qingyang and Yan'an (coordinates used).
